higher_order_functions.notes: Functions as values, as arguments, as key functions (B06 left key=<own function> here) and map/filter. Returning functions is owned by closures.function_factories. Storing functions as dict values (100 Days calculator) was not written because dicts are B07 (parallel); a stitching pass may add a KP to functions_are_values or a B07 practice item. map/filter use lists and range only; map/filter vs comprehensions is B07's to compare. Reconciliation: functions stored in a dict (dispatch tables, 100 Days calculator) is now dispatch_tables.

lambda_functions.notes: key=lambda (deferred by B06 sorting) is lambda_as_argument KP1-2, which encompasses sorting.sort_tuples_and_keys. Sorting dict items with key=lambda kv: kv[1] belongs to B07 dictionaries and can encompass lambda_as_argument.

closures.notes: Owns enclosing scope, LEGB and nonlocal (deferred by B05 scope). The late-binding trap (lambdas made in a loop) is function_factories KP4. nonlocal_state is non-core: decorators do not depend on it.

currying.notes: One non-core topic (bootdev only). Includes functools.partial, imported with a single memorised from-import line, as B06 did with import copy, ahead of B13 modules_imports.

decorators.notes: General function decorators only. @property, @classmethod and @staticmethod belong to the OOP batch (B11), Flask @app.route to the web batch, @pytest.fixture to B09 lib_pytest, @contextmanager to B10 context_managers; all can build on decorators.at_syntax. Timing decorators need the time module (B13) and retry decorators need try/except (B09), so neither is used here. general_wrappers needs args_kwargs.unpack_in_calls.

generators.notes: All non-core, because they build on iteration.iter_and_next (non-core in B04). If iteration becomes core, yield_values and generator_expressions are good core candidates. generator_expressions has pending concept:list_comprehensions (B07, parallel); B05 asked B07 to cover any()/all() with generator expressions, so the stitching pass should check B07 did not also write a generator-expression topic (keep this one, have B07 encompass it or vice versa). send(), throw() and close() (codecademy only) were left out. Generators as context managers (@contextmanager) are B10. itertools is B07. Reconciliation: iteration.iter_and_next, yield_values and generator_expressions are core; lazy_and_infinite and pipelines stay non-core.

args_kwargs.notes: star_kwargs has pending concept:dictionaries (B07): kwargs is a dict, and only dict literal printing, d[key] and looping over keys are used. unpack_in_calls teaches f(*seq) from scratch so it can stay core, and encompasses B06 unpacking.star_unpacking (non-core) as non_ancestor. The keyword-only / positional-only markers (* and /) that B05 deferred are a non-core topic. Reconciliation: unpack_in_calls now depends on unpacking.star_unpacking (promoted to core) instead of re-teaching * in calls from scratch.

recursion.notes: Seven topics despite 4 courses because those teach it deep and it is a classic failure point. nested_lists is non-core with pending concept:nested_data_structures (B07) and uses type(x) == list, since isinstance is B11. Memoising with a hand-written dict is left to the stitching pass or a later algorithms batch (dicts are B07); memoize_with_cache uses functools.cache instead. Recursion on trees, binary search, merge sort and the static site generator belong to later data structures/algorithms batches and should depend on recursion_on_sequences and multiple_recursive_calls. Mathematical induction was not given a topic here. Reconciliation: nested_lists now uses isinstance(item, list) (objects_methods.isinstance_checks) and depends on nested_data_structures.grid_index_and_loop.

pure_functions.notes: One non-core topic (bootdev only); builds on B05 decomposition.one_job_per_function as B05 asked. B09 unit_testing could list it as a motivating prerequisite.

functional_programming.notes: Problem-based, non-core. Its parts (higher_order_functions, lambda_functions, closures, pure_functions) own their own topics. Comprehensions as the idiomatic alternative to map/filter are B07. Sum types (bootdev) need classes/enums and are left to B11.

topics.title: Functions are values: naming, storing and printing them
topics.summary: Treat a function as a value: give it a second name, keep functions in a list and loop over them, and tell f (the function) from f() (its result).

knowledge_points.title: A second name for the same function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def shout(text):
    return text.upper() + "!"

yell = shout
print(yell("hi"))  # HI!
yell = shout copies no code: both names now refer to the same function object.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what calls through a second name return; fill in the assignment that makes a new name work.

knowledge_points.title: f is the function, f() is its result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(len("abc"))  # 3
print(len)  # <built-in function len>
result = len
print(result)  # <built-in function len>
Without parentheses nothing is called: you get the function itself.
knowledge_points.practice: For each line, decide whether it prints a result or a function object.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting the parentheses is a silent bug
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the missing call in short snippets that print the wrong answer.

knowledge_points.title: Keeping functions in a list
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of looping over a list of functions; write a loop that applies each function in a list to one value.

topics.title: Functions in a dictionary: dispatch tables
topics.summary: Store functions as dictionary values, pick and call one by key (for example from user input), replace an if/elif chain on a string with a lookup and a default, and keep every function in the table callable the same way.

knowledge_points.title: Functions as dictionary values
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of calls through a dict of functions; add an entry for a new operation.

knowledge_points.title: Choose the function from what the user types
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the calculator for several inputs, including an unknown symbol; write the lookup-and-call lines.

knowledge_points.title: Replace an if/elif chain with a lookup and a default
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite an elif chain that compares one string as a dispatch table; predict get() with and without a default.

knowledge_points.title: Same arguments for every entry; store the function, not its result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def square(n):
    return n * n
operations = {"square": square, "add": add}
print(operations["add"](2, 3))  # 5
operations["square"](2, 3)  # TypeError: square() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given
{"square": square()}  # TypeError: square() missing 1 required positional argument: 'n'
The caller treats every entry alike, so every function must accept the same arguments; square() would call it while building the dict.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the entry that breaks the table and fix its parameters; fix a table that stores call results.

topics.notes: Added in reconciliation (gap: B08 and B07 each left 'functions in a dict' to the other). Snippets run with Python 3.13 (input answers 7, *, 2). Used by cli_applications.command_loop, web_development.how_web_apps_work (routing), event_driven_programming and function_calling.dispatch_tool_calls.

topics.title: Passing a function to another function
topics.summary: Write functions that take another function as a parameter and call it, and pass functions (not their results) as arguments.

knowledge_points.title: A parameter can receive a function
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of apply-style calls with built-in and own functions.

knowledge_points.title: Calling the passed function more than once
knowledge_points.practice: Trace apply_twice and apply_n_times with different functions; write apply_three_times.

knowledge_points.title: Pass the function, not its result
knowledge_points.practice: Spot and fix calls that pass a result instead of a function; predict the error message.

knowledge_points.title: A general helper that takes a test function
knowledge_points.practice: Write count_if or keep_if style helpers and call them with two different test functions.

topics.title: Sorting and choosing with your own key function
topics.summary: Pass your own function as key= to sorted(), max() and min(), including tie-breaking keys that return a tuple.

knowledge_points.title: key= with a function you wrote
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def last_letter(word):
    return word[-1]

print(sorted(["plum", "kiwi", "fig"], key=last_letter))
# ['fig', 'kiwi', 'plum']
sorted calls last_letter on every item and orders by the results g, i, m.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order produced by a given key function; write a key function for a stated order.

knowledge_points.title: Key functions for records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def price(item):
    return item[1]

items = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5), ("jam", 2)]
print(sorted(items, key=price))
# [('jam', 2), ('tea', 3), ('cake', 5)]
The key picks the field to sort by; the records themselves are returned whole.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the key function that sorts records by a named field, then sort in reverse with reverse=True.

knowledge_points.title: max() and min() with key= return the item, not the key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def price(item):
    return item[1]

items = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5), ("jam", 2)]
print(max(items, key=price))  # ('cake', 5)
print(min(items, key=price)[0])  # jam
The key is only used to compare; you get back the whole record.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict max/min results with a key; fix code that expects max to return the key value.

knowledge_points.title: Breaking ties with a tuple key
knowledge_points.practice: Write a key that sorts by one field and breaks ties by another; predict sorts where ties occur.

topics.title: Transforming and selecting with map() and filter()
topics.summary: Use map() to apply a function to every item and filter() to keep the items that pass a test, converting the lazy result with list().

knowledge_points.title: map() applies a function to every item
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

print(list(map(double, [1, 2, 3])))  # [2, 4, 6]
print(list(map(int, ["4", "5"])))  # [4, 5]
map(f, items) does the job of a loop that appends f(item) for every item.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict map results; rewrite an append loop as list(map(...)).

knowledge_points.title: map() gives a map object that is used up once
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

m = map(double, [1, 2])
print(list(m))  # [2, 4]
print(list(m))  # []
print(m) would show <map object at 0x...>; the values are produced on demand and only once.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a second list() or loop over the same map object gives; fix code that prints a map object.

knowledge_points.title: filter() keeps the items that pass a test
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def is_even(n):
    return n % 2 == 0

print(list(filter(is_even, range(10))))  # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
filter calls the test on each item and keeps those where it returns True.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filter results; write a test function and a filter call for a stated condition.

knowledge_points.title: Parsing a line with map(), then filtering
knowledge_points.worked_example:
line = "3 8 1 6"
numbers = list(map(int, line.split()))
print(numbers)  # [3, 8, 1, 6]
print(list(filter(is_even, numbers)))  # [8, 6]
map(int, text.split()) is the standard way to parse numbers from one line of input; filter then keeps the ones you want (is_even from KP3).
knowledge_points.practice: Parse lines of numbers with map(int, ...split()); chain a filter on the result; fill in the missing function names.

topics.title: Writing small functions with lambda
topics.summary: Write lambda expressions with one or more parameters, know the body is a single expression that is returned, and pass a lambda straight into a call.

knowledge_points.title: lambda parameters: expression
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

double_too = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(5), double_too(5))  # 10 10
A lambda is an unnamed function; the expression after the colon is returned.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert one-line defs to lambdas and back; predict calls to a lambda.

knowledge_points.title: Several parameters, or none
knowledge_points.worked_example:
add = lambda a, b: a + b
print(add(2, 3))  # 5
get_answer = lambda: 42
print(get_answer())  # 42
Parameters are separated by commas, exactly as in def; a lambda with no parameters is still called with ().
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of multi-parameter lambdas; write a lambda for a given two-input formula.

knowledge_points.title: One expression only: use a conditional expression for choices
knowledge_points.worked_example:
sign = lambda n: "negative" if n < 0 else "not negative"
print(sign(-4))  # negative
bad = lambda x: return x  # SyntaxError: invalid syntax
No statements (return, if blocks, assignments) are allowed in a lambda body; x if c else y is an expression, so it is.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which lambdas are valid; rewrite an if/else def as a lambda with a conditional expression.

knowledge_points.title: Passing a lambda straight into a call
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a lambda argument so a call produces a target value; predict calls of apply-style helpers with lambdas.

topics.title: Lambdas as sort keys and with map() and filter()
topics.summary: Use lambdas inline as key= for sorted/max/min and as the function for map() and filter(), and know when a named def is clearer.

knowledge_points.title: key=lambda to sort records
knowledge_points.worked_example:
items = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5), ("jam", 2)]
print(sorted(items, key=lambda item: item[1]))
# [('jam', 2), ('tea', 3), ('cake', 5)]
The lambda replaces a one-line key function defined elsewhere.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the key=lambda that sorts by a named field or computed value; predict the resulting order.

knowledge_points.title: max() and min() with a lambda key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [("ana", 81), ("bo", 92), ("cy", 77)]
best = max(scores, key=lambda s: s[1])
print(best[0])  # bo
Remember max returns the whole record; index it afterwards for the part you want.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the best/worst record by a field; fix code that indexes the wrong part of the result.

knowledge_points.title: Lambdas with map() and filter()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["hi", "hello", "hey", "howdy"]
print(list(filter(lambda w: len(w) > 3, words)))  # ['hello', 'howdy']
print(list(map(lambda w: w[0].upper(), words)))  # ['H', 'H', 'H', 'H']
filter's lambda must return True/False; map's lambda returns the new value.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict map/filter calls with lambdas; write one that keeps or transforms items by a rule.

knowledge_points.title: When a def is clearer than a lambda
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, -1, 4]
print(list(filter(lambda n: n if n > 0, nums)))  # SyntaxError: expected 'else' after 'if' expression
A lambda cannot hold an if statement; once logic needs several steps or a name worth reading, write a def.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix broken lambdas; choose between lambda and def for described tasks.

topics.title: Functions inside functions and the enclosing scope
topics.summary: Define a helper inside another function, read the outer function's variables from it, and predict name lookup with the LEGB rule.

knowledge_points.title: A def inside a def
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def greet_all():
    def greet(name):
        print("Hi", name)
    greet("Ana")
    greet("Bo")

greet_all()  # Hi Ana / Hi Bo
The inner def runs each time greet_all runs, creating a helper only greet_all uses.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output and call order for nested defs.

knowledge_points.title: The inner function can read the outer function's variables
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results when an inner function reads outer variables and parameters.

knowledge_points.title: The inner function does not exist outside
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which calls work and which raise NameError.

knowledge_points.title: Lookup order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which of several same-named variables a line reads; fix a program that shadowed a built-in.

topics.title: Returning functions: closures and function factories
topics.summary: Write a function that builds and returns another function which remembers values from where it was made, and avoid the late-binding trap.

knowledge_points.title: Return the inner function itself
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_greeter(greeting):
    def greet(name):
        return f"{greeting}, {name}!"
    return greet

hello = make_greeter("Hello")
print(hello("Ana"))  # Hello, Ana!
return greet (no parentheses) hands back the function; it still knows greeting after make_greeter has finished.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict calls to returned functions; fix a factory that returns greet() instead of greet.

knowledge_points.title: Each call makes a separate closure
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_multiplier(n):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * n
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)
print(double(5), triple(5))  # 10 15
Each call of make_multiplier has its own n, and each returned function remembers its own.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results from several functions made by one factory; write a factory for a described family of functions.

knowledge_points.title: Returning a lambda
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_adder(n):
    return lambda x: x + n

add5 = make_adder(5)
print(add5(10))  # 15
print(make_adder(1)(1))  # 2
A lambda closes over n just like a def; make_adder(1)(1) builds and calls in one line.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite def-based factories with lambdas; predict chained calls like f(a)(b).

knowledge_points.title: Late binding: closures see the variable, not its old value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = 2
times_n = lambda x: x * n
n = 10
print(times_n(3))  # 30, not 6

m = 2
times_m = lambda x, m=m: x * m
m = 10
print(times_m(3))  # 6
times_n reads n when it is called, not when it was made; a default m=m freezes the value at creation, because defaults are computed once.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results when a captured variable changes after the function is made (including functions made in a loop); fix the bug with a default argument or a factory call.

topics.title: Closures that remember state with nonlocal
topics.summary: Use nonlocal to update a variable of the enclosing function, build independent counters, and know when mutation needs no nonlocal.

knowledge_points.title: nonlocal lets the inner function rebind an outer variable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

c = make_counter()
print(c(), c(), c())  # 1 2 3
count lives on between calls because the closure keeps it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values returned by repeated calls; fill in the missing nonlocal line.

knowledge_points.title: Without nonlocal: UnboundLocalError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

c = make_counter()
c()  # UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value
Assigning to count makes it local to counter, exactly like the global case; nonlocal is the fix.
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the missing nonlocal; predict which snippets raise UnboundLocalError.

knowledge_points.title: Every closure has its own state
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def counter():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return counter

a = make_counter()
b = make_counter()
a(); a()
print(a(), b())  # 3 1
Unlike a global counter, two counters made by the factory never interfere.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace interleaved calls to several counters; write a factory for a running total.

knowledge_points.title: Changing a captured list needs no nonlocal
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_logger():
    log = []
    def add(msg):
        log.append(msg)
        return log
    return add

add = make_logger()
add("start")
print(add("stop"))  # ['start', 'stop']
nonlocal is needed only to rebind a name (=, +=); calling a method on the object is not rebinding.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which inner functions need nonlocal; predict outputs of closures that mutate a list.

topics.title: Currying and partial application
topics.summary: Turn a multi-argument function into a chain of one-argument functions, fix some arguments to make specialised functions, and use functools.partial.

knowledge_points.title: f(a, b) becomes f(a)(b)
knowledge_points.practice: Convert two-argument functions to curried form; predict chained calls.

knowledge_points.title: Fixing one argument makes a specialised function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def power(exponent):
    return lambda base: base ** exponent

square = power(2)
cube = power(3)
print(list(map(cube, [1, 2, 3])))  # [1, 8, 27]
Supplying the first argument early gives a one-argument function, ready for map or key=.
knowledge_points.practice: Make specialised functions from a curried one and pass them to map or sorted.

knowledge_points.title: Three levels of currying
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def volume(length):
    return lambda width: lambda height: length * width * height

print(volume(2)(3)(4))  # 24
base_2x3 = volume(2)(3)
print(base_2x3(10))  # 60
Each call consumes one argument; stopping early gives a partly applied function.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of partly applied chains; count how many calls are needed to get a number.

knowledge_points.title: functools.partial does it for any function
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import partial

from_binary = partial(int, base=2)
print(from_binary("101"))  # 5
print(partial(pow, 2)(5))  # 32
partial(f, fixed args) returns a new function with those arguments already filled in.
knowledge_points.practice: Write partial calls that build a requested function; predict their results.

topics.title: Wrapping a function to add behaviour
topics.summary: Write a function that takes a function and returns a wrapper which runs extra code around the original, and replace the original with it.

knowledge_points.title: A wrapper runs code before and after
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed lines when a wrapped function is called; put the lines of a wrapper in order.

knowledge_points.title: Replacing a function with its wrapped version
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output after reassigning a name to its wrapped version; predict what happens when it is wrapped twice.

knowledge_points.title: Passing the argument through and returning the result
knowledge_points.practice: Write a wrapper that changes a one-argument function's result (round it, upper-case it, double it).

knowledge_points.title: A wrapper that forgets to return gives None
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix wrappers that lose the result; predict their printed output.

topics.title: Decorators with @
topics.summary: Apply a decorator with @, know it runs once when the def runs, and predict the order of stacked decorators.

knowledge_points.title: @decorator means f = decorator(f)
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite explicit reassignment as @ and back; predict output of decorated calls.

knowledge_points.title: The decorator runs once, when the def runs
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the full output order of programs that define and then call decorated functions.

knowledge_points.title: Stacked decorators apply bottom-up
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of two stacked decorators in both orders; choose the order that gives a target output.

knowledge_points.title: A decorator that guards the input
knowledge_points.practice: Write a decorator that checks or adjusts its argument before calling the original.

topics.title: Decorators for any function: *args, **kwargs and functools.wraps
topics.summary: Write a wrapper that accepts and forwards any arguments with *args and **kwargs, and keep the original's name with functools.wraps.

knowledge_points.title: wrapper(*args, **kwargs) works for any signature
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what the wrapper collects for different calls; fill in the forwarding line.

knowledge_points.title: A fixed-size wrapper breaks other functions
knowledge_points.practice: Read the error, then fix the wrapper so it handles any arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Keep the name with functools.wraps
knowledge_points.practice: Predict __name__ with and without @wraps; add the missing @wraps line.

knowledge_points.title: A reusable decorator that changes results
knowledge_points.practice: Write a general decorator (round, clamp, upper-case) and apply it to functions with different parameters.

topics.title: Decorators that take arguments
topics.summary: Write a decorator factory such as @repeat(3), predict how @name(args) is evaluated, and fix the missing-parentheses bug.

knowledge_points.title: A function that returns a decorator
knowledge_points.practice: Put the three nested defs in order; predict the output for different settings.

knowledge_points.title: @repeat(3) is called first, then applied
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite @factory(args) lines as plain assignments; predict printed setup messages.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting the parentheses
knowledge_points.practice: Diagnose and fix factory decorators used without arguments.

topics.title: Generator functions and yield
topics.summary: Write a generator function with yield, step through it with next() and for, and know that a generator is used up after one pass.

knowledge_points.title: yield turns a function into a generator
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a for loop over a generator prints; write a generator for a described sequence.

knowledge_points.title: Calling it runs nothing yet; next() runs to the next yield
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def count_up(n):
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        yield i
        i += 1

g = count_up(2)
print(next(g), next(g))  # 1 2
next(g)  # StopIteration
count_up(2) only creates a generator object; next() runs the body until the next yield, and StopIteration means it finished.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict a sequence of next() calls, including the one that raises StopIteration.

knowledge_points.title: yield pauses; return ends
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def steps():
    print("A")
    yield 1
    print("B")
    yield 2
    print("C")

for value in steps():
    print(value)  # A 1 B 2 C, one per line
Local state and position are kept between values; return (or reaching the end) stops the generator for good.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace interleaved prints from a generator and its loop; contrast with a function that returns a list.

knowledge_points.title: A generator is used up after one pass
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def count_up(n):
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        yield i
        i += 1

g = count_up(3)
print(list(g))  # [1, 2, 3]
print(list(g))  # []
list(g) collects every value; the second pass finds nothing. Call count_up(3) again for a fresh generator.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of reusing a generator; fix code that loops twice over one generator.

topics.title: Lazy and infinite generators
topics.summary: Write generators that produce values only when asked, including endless ones consumed with break, and generators that yield only matching values.

knowledge_points.title: An endless generator and a loop that breaks
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where a loop over an endless generator stops; write the loop that finds the first value passing a test.

knowledge_points.title: Taking the first n values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def naturals():
    n = 1
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 1

g = naturals()
first = []
for _ in range(3):
    first.append(next(g))
print(first)  # [1, 2, 3]
print(next(g))  # 4
next() continues the same generator, so the following call carries on from 4.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict values when next() is called on a generator between loops; write a take(g, n) helper.

knowledge_points.title: Yielding only some values
knowledge_points.practice: Write generators that produce primes, evens or matching words; predict their first few values.

knowledge_points.title: return stops a generator early
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output of generators with an early return; fix one that uses break where the caller expects it to stop.

topics.title: Generator expressions
topics.summary: Write (expr for x in items) and (expr for x in items if cond) and pass them straight to sum(), max() and similar built-ins.

knowledge_points.title: Parentheses make a generator expression
knowledge_points.worked_example:
squares = (x * x for x in range(5))
print(squares)  # <generator object <genexpr> at 0x...>
print(list(squares))  # [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]
It is a one-line generator: nothing is computed until something asks for values.
knowledge_points.practice: Convert short generator functions to generator expressions; predict their contents with list().

knowledge_points.title: Drop the brackets of a comprehension inside a call
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(max([len(w) for w in words]))  # 6: builds a list first
print(max(len(w) for w in words))    # 6: no list is ever built
print(sum(x * x for x in range(1, 4)))  # 14
Inside a call's own parentheses no extra pair is needed; the values arrive one at a time.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite comprehensions passed to sum(), max() and any() as generator expressions; compare with the equivalent map(); predict results.

knowledge_points.title: Filtering with if
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(sum(1 for w in words if len(w) > 3))  # 2
The if keeps only matching items; sum(1 for ...) counts them.
knowledge_points.practice: Count and total items that meet a condition with a single expression.

knowledge_points.title: Used up after one pass, like any generator
knowledge_points.worked_example:
evens = (n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 0)
print(sum(evens))  # 6
print(sum(evens))  # 0
The second sum finds the generator empty; build a list if you need the values twice.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict repeated use of one generator expression; fix code that reuses it.

topics.title: Chaining generators into pipelines
topics.summary: Connect generators so each one consumes another's output, and delegate to another iterable with yield from.

knowledge_points.title: One generator feeding another
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of two- and three-stage pipelines; write a stage for a described step.

knowledge_points.title: yield from hands over to another iterable
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def both(a, b):
    yield from a
    yield from b

print(list(both([1, 2], "ab")))  # [1, 2, 'a', 'b']
yield from x is short for: for item in x: yield item.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite for/yield loops with yield from; predict the combined output.

knowledge_points.title: A text-cleaning pipeline
knowledge_points.worked_example:
lines = ["  apple ", "", " pear", "   "]
stripped = (line.strip() for line in lines)
non_empty = (line for line in stripped if line)
print(list(non_empty))  # ['apple', 'pear']
Each stage is one small step; nothing runs until list() pulls values through.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the stages of a pipeline to produce a target result; add a stage that upper-cases.

topics.title: Any number of positional arguments: *args
topics.summary: Define functions with *args, use the tuple it collects, and combine it with ordinary and keyword-only parameters.

knowledge_points.title: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def show(*args):
    print(args)

show(1, 2, 3)  # (1, 2, 3)
show()  # ()
The star in the def means: pack all positional arguments into one tuple; the name args is only a convention.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the tuple collected for different calls, including no arguments.

knowledge_points.title: Looping over args
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def total(*numbers):
    result = 0
    for n in numbers:
        result += n
    return result

print(total(4, 5, 6))  # 15
print(total())  # 0
args is an ordinary tuple: loop over it, index it, take its len.
knowledge_points.practice: Write *args functions such as largest(*nums) or average(*nums); handle the no-argument case.

knowledge_points.title: Ordinary parameters first, then *args
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which arguments land in which parameter; fill in a def line for a described call.

knowledge_points.title: Parameters after *args must be passed by keyword
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of calls with and without the keyword; fix calls that pass the option by position.

topics.title: Any number of keyword arguments: **kwargs
topics.summary: Define functions with **kwargs, read the dict it collects, and order ordinary, *args, keyword-only and **kwargs parameters correctly.

knowledge_points.title: **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dict
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the dict collected for different calls.

knowledge_points.title: Reading the collected values
knowledge_points.practice: Write functions that print or build text from their keyword arguments; look up one expected key.

knowledge_points.title: The full order: normal, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs
knowledge_points.practice: Predict where each argument goes; put the parameters of a def in a legal order.

knowledge_points.title: Positional arguments cannot go into **kwargs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def show(**kwargs):
    print(kwargs)

show("Ana")  # TypeError: show() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
**kwargs only accepts name=value arguments; add *args if positional ones are needed too.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise TypeError; fix the def or the call.

topics.title: Spreading a list or dict into a call with * and **
topics.summary: Unpack a list or tuple into positional arguments with * and a dict into keyword arguments with **, and forward arguments from one function to another.

knowledge_points.title: * in a call spreads a sequence into arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

size = [3, 4]
print(area(*size))  # 12
Just as print(*nums) spreads a list into print, area(*size) is area(3, 4); without the star, size would be one argument.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict calls that use *; fix a call that passes a list where separate arguments are needed.

knowledge_points.title: The counts must match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

print(area(*[1, 2, 3]))  # TypeError: area() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
The star spreads every item; the function still decides how many it accepts.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which spread calls succeed; predict the error message for the others.

knowledge_points.title: ** in a call spreads a dict into keyword arguments
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite keyword calls using a dict and **; predict the result.

knowledge_points.title: Forwarding arguments to another function
knowledge_points.practice: Write a forwarding function; predict results of forwarded calls.

topics.title: Keyword-only and positional-only parameters: * and /
topics.summary: Use a bare * to force keyword arguments and / to forbid them, and read these markers in function signatures.

knowledge_points.title: A bare * makes the following parameters keyword-only
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def make_box(*, width, height):
    return width * height

print(make_box(width=2, height=5))  # 10
make_box(2, 5)  # TypeError: make_box() takes 0 positional arguments but 2 were given
Forcing names stops callers mixing up arguments of the same type.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls succeed; add * to a def so a call must name its options.

knowledge_points.title: / makes the earlier parameters positional-only
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def half(x, /):
    return x / 2

print(half(8))  # 4.0
half(x=8)  # TypeError: half() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'x'
Parameters before / cannot be named in the call, so their names can change freely later.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which calls raise TypeError for a def using /.

knowledge_points.title: Reading signatures with / and *
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False)
print(sorted([3, 1, 2], reverse=True))  # [3, 2, 1]
sorted([3, 1, 2], True)  # TypeError: sorted expected 1 argument, got 2
help() shows signatures like this: iterable is positional-only, key and reverse are keyword-only.
knowledge_points.practice: Given a signature, decide which calls are legal; write the def line for a described signature.

topics.title: Recursion: functions that call themselves
topics.summary: Write a recursive function with a base case that stops and a recursive case that moves toward it, for countdowns, sums, factorials and powers.

knowledge_points.title: A function that calls itself
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the output of short recursive printing functions; identify the base case and the recursive call.

knowledge_points.title: Base case returns, recursive case builds on a smaller call
knowledge_points.practice: Predict return values; fill in the base case or the recursive expression.

knowledge_points.title: Factorial from its definition
knowledge_points.practice: Write factorial and similar product functions; predict results for small inputs.

knowledge_points.title: Writing a function from a recurrence
knowledge_points.practice: Given a rule in words, write the recursive function (power, multiply by adding, count digits).

topics.title: Tracing recursive calls
topics.summary: Trace recursive calls with a call stack: each call's own variables, work done before versus after the recursive call, and how results return.

knowledge_points.title: Each call has its own n
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in a trace table of calls and their n values; count how many calls a given input makes.

knowledge_points.title: Results return back up the stack
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the return value of each call in order; predict the final result.

knowledge_points.title: Work before or after the recursive call
knowledge_points.practice: Predict output order for functions that print before, after, or both.

topics.title: Fixing recursion bugs: missing base cases and lost results
topics.summary: Recognise and fix RecursionError from a missing or unreachable base case, None from a missing return, and inputs too deep for recursion.

knowledge_points.title: No base case: RecursionError
knowledge_points.practice: Spot which recursive functions can never stop; add the missing base case.

knowledge_points.title: A base case the input never reaches
knowledge_points.practice: Trace inputs that jump over the base case; fix the condition.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting to return the recursive result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def sum_to(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    n + sum_to(n - 1)  # bug: no return

print(sum_to(1))  # None
print(sum_to(2))  # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'NoneType'
The recursive case computed a value and threw it away, so the call returned None.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a function missing return gives; fix it.

knowledge_points.title: Correct but too deep: use a loop
knowledge_points.practice: Decide which inputs exceed the limit; rewrite a simple recursive function as a loop.

topics.title: Recursion on strings and lists
topics.summary: Solve string and list problems recursively by handling the first item (or both ends) and recursing on the rest via slicing.

knowledge_points.title: First character plus the rest
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of recursive string functions; write count_vowels(s) recursively.

knowledge_points.title: First item plus the rest of a list
knowledge_points.practice: Write recursive length, total and maximum of a list; trace one call chain.

knowledge_points.title: Working from both ends
knowledge_points.practice: Predict palindrome checks; fill in the missing base case.

knowledge_points.title: Building a new list recursively
knowledge_points.practice: Write recursive filters and transforms that return lists; compare with the loop version.

topics.title: Branching recursion: Fibonacci and Towers of Hanoi
topics.summary: Write recursive functions that make two calls per step, trace their call trees, and recognise why naive versions grow exponentially.

knowledge_points.title: Two recursive calls and two base cases
knowledge_points.practice: Predict small Fibonacci values; write a recursive function with two calls (e.g. a 1-or-2-steps staircase count).

knowledge_points.title: The call tree
knowledge_points.practice: Count the calls in a call tree; list the calls in the order they happen.

knowledge_points.title: Why naive branching recursion gets slow
knowledge_points.practice: Estimate how the call count grows as n grows; choose which functions will be slow.

knowledge_points.title: Towers of Hanoi: solving by trusting the smaller call
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def hanoi(n, start, end, spare):
    if n == 0:
        return
    hanoi(n - 1, start, spare, end)
    print("move", n, start, "->", end)
    hanoi(n - 1, spare, end, start)

hanoi(2, "A", "C", "B")  # move 1 A -> B / move 2 A -> C / move 1 B -> C
Move n - 1 disks out of the way, move the biggest, move the n - 1 back on top: assume the smaller call works.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the moves for 2-3 disks; count moves for n disks (2^n - 1).

topics.title: Recursion on nested lists
topics.summary: Process lists that contain lists to any depth (sum, flatten, depth) by recursing whenever an item is itself a list.

knowledge_points.title: Items that are lists themselves
knowledge_points.worked_example:
data = [1, [2, 3], [4, [5]]]
for item in data:
    print(item, isinstance(item, list))
# 1 False / [2, 3] True / [4, [5]] True
A loop sees only the top level; isinstance(item, list) tells which items need going into.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict len() and the type checks of nested lists; count top-level items.

knowledge_points.title: Summing at every depth
knowledge_points.practice: Write nested_sum / nested_count; trace which calls are made for a small input.

knowledge_points.title: Flattening into one list
knowledge_points.practice: Fix a flatten that uses append for sub-lists; predict flatten results.

knowledge_points.title: Measuring the depth
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the depth of given lists; write the function that finds the largest number at any depth.

topics.title: Speeding up recursion: caching and loops
topics.summary: Make branching recursion fast by caching results, with functools.cache or a hand-written dict, or by rewriting it as a loop.

knowledge_points.title: The same subproblems are solved again and again
knowledge_points.practice: Count repeated calls in a call tree; choose which inputs are recomputed.

knowledge_points.title: @cache remembers results
knowledge_points.practice: Add @cache to slow recursive functions; predict how many times the body runs for a given input.

knowledge_points.title: Or count up with a loop
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def fib(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a

print(fib(10))  # 55
Building from the base cases upward needs only the last two values and no recursion at all.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the two-variable loop; rewrite another branching recursion (staircase count) as a loop.

knowledge_points.title: Memoising by hand with a dict
knowledge_points.practice: Fill in the lookup and store lines of a memoised function; trace which calls are answered from the dict.

topics.title: Pure functions and side effects
topics.summary: Tell pure functions (same inputs, same output, nothing else changed) from ones with side effects or hidden inputs, and rewrite impure functions as pure ones.

knowledge_points.title: Same inputs, same output, nothing else changes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def area(w, h):
    return w * h

print(area(3, 4), area(3, 4))  # 12 12
area is pure: its result depends only on its arguments and calling it changes nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify short functions as pure or not, giving the reason.

knowledge_points.title: Side effects: printing, input, changing globals, mutating arguments
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_item(cart, item):
    cart.append(item)
    return cart

mine = ["tea"]
add_item(mine, "jam")
print(mine)  # ['tea', 'jam']
The caller's list changed: that is a side effect, even though the function also returns a value.
knowledge_points.practice: Identify every side effect in given functions; predict the state of variables after the calls.

knowledge_points.title: Hidden inputs: reading a global
knowledge_points.worked_example:
rate = 0.2

def with_tax(price):
    return price * (1 + rate)

print(with_tax(10))  # 12.0
rate = 0.5
print(with_tax(10))  # 15.0
Same argument, different result: the global is an input the call does not show.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results after a global changes; fix the function by making the value a parameter.

knowledge_points.title: Rewriting an impure function as a pure one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def add_item(cart, item):
    return cart + [item]

mine = ["tea"]
new = add_item(mine, "jam")
print(mine, new)  # ['tea'] ['tea', 'jam']
Return a new value instead of changing the old one; pure functions are easy to test and reuse.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite functions that mutate, print or read globals so they are pure.

topics.title: From loops to map, filter and built-ins: declarative style
topics.summary: Rewrite imperative accumulation loops as compositions of filter, map, sorted and sum, without mutating data, and judge which version reads better.

knowledge_points.title: Same task, two styles
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 8, 1, 6]
total = 0
for n in nums:
    if n > 2:
        total += n * n
print(total)  # 109
print(sum(map(lambda n: n * n, filter(lambda n: n > 2, nums))))  # 109
The loop says how to compute step by step; the second line says what: square the large ones and add.
knowledge_points.practice: Match loops to equivalent map/filter/sum expressions; predict both versions.

knowledge_points.title: Building a pipeline step by step
knowledge_points.worked_example:
words = ["Pear", "fig", "Apple", "kiwi"]
lower = map(str.lower, words)
long = filter(lambda w: len(w) > 3, lower)
print(sorted(long))  # ['apple', 'kiwi', 'pear']
Each step takes the previous result; read the pipeline in order.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of a pipeline (Parsons); write one for a described transformation.

knowledge_points.title: No mutation: produce new values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
scores = [70, 95, 82]
ranked = sorted(scores, reverse=True)
print(scores, ranked)  # [70, 95, 82] [95, 82, 70]
sorted returns a new list and leaves scores alone; sort() would have changed it.
knowledge_points.practice: Replace mutating steps (sort, append, +=) with expressions that return new values.

knowledge_points.title: When the loop reads better
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# Hard to read:
# print(list(map(lambda p: p[0], filter(lambda p: p[1] > 50 and p[0] != "x", pairs))))
pairs = [("a", 60), ("x", 90), ("b", 40)]
for name, score in pairs:
    if score > 50 and name != "x":
        print(name)  # a
Deeply nested map/filter with long lambdas is harder to read than a short loop; pick the clearer one.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the clearer version for several tasks and justify the choice.

topics.title: Folding a list into one value with reduce()
topics.summary: Use functools.reduce with and without an initial value, trace how it combines items, and prefer sum/max/join when they exist.

knowledge_points.title: reduce combines items two at a time
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import reduce

print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [1, 2, 3, 4]))  # 10
# ((1 + 2) + 3) + 4
The function gets the result so far and the next item, like an accumulator loop.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the accumulator through each step; predict the result.

knowledge_points.title: An initial value, and the empty-list error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import reduce

print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc * x, [2, 3, 4], 1))  # 24
print(reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [], 0))  # 0
reduce(lambda acc, x: acc + x, [])  # TypeError: reduce() of empty iterable with no initial value
The third argument is the starting accumulator; it also makes empty input safe.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results with and without an initial value; fix a reduce that crashes on empty input.

knowledge_points.title: Reductions that are not sums
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from functools import reduce

words = ["a", "bb", "ccc"]
print(reduce(lambda acc, w: acc + len(w), words, 0))  # 6
print(reduce(lambda a, b: a if a > b else b, [3, 9, 2]))  # 9
The initial value can be a different type from the items (an int for a list of strings).
knowledge_points.practice: Write reduce calls for product, maximum and total length.

knowledge_points.title: Prefer the built-in when there is one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
nums = [3, 9, 2]
print(sum(nums), max(nums), "-".join(["a", "b"]))  # 14 9 a-b
sum, max, min and join are reductions with names; reach for reduce only when none fits.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the clearest tool (built-in, reduce or loop) for described reductions.
